key_insight: Machine-learned dynamics show that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces are far less mobile than in bulk because surface geometry removes most hopping pathways and vacancies trap nearby electrons.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can exhibit much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for designing oxide-based catalysts, photovoltaics, and energy-storage devices.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a redox-active oxide surface.
Ran several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways and vacancy-induced changes in the free-energy landscape.
evidence_signal: The study uses nanosecond-scale simulations across multiple temperatures to compare surface and bulk polaron mobility, revealing orders-of-magnitude suppression at the reduced surface.
watch_item: The approach is validated on a specific oxide surface, so transferability to other defect chemistries and more complex real surfaces still needs careful checking.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
